pedagogy.summary: An inequality compares expressions and, unlike an equation, its solution is a RANGE (a set) of values, not a single value. On a number line that range is shown by a circle at the boundary — open/hollow for strict < or > (boundary excluded), closed/filled for inclusive ≤ or ≥ (boundary included) — with an arrow or segment covering the values that satisfy it. Solving uses the same inverse operations as equations. The representational competence is translating fluently among worded constraint, inequality symbol and number-line diagram; it is best taught by tying the circle style to boundary inclusion, the arrow to the satisfying set, and rehearsing worded phrases such as 'at least' and 'at most'.
bestPractices: Distinguish strict from inclusive explicitly: open circle = boundary NOT included (<, >), closed circle = boundary included (≤, ≥), tied to whether the boundary value itself satisfies the statement.
Represent the solution as a SET (arrow/segment), not a point; test a value inside and outside the range to confirm which side to shade.
Rehearse worded-constraint translation: 'at least 12' → x ≥ 12, 'at most'/'no more than' → ≤, 'more than' → strict >.
Solve inequalities with the same inverse operations as equations (for KS3 cases like 3x + 1 < 10) and read the result back onto the number line.
(KS4 extension) flag that multiplying or dividing both sides by a NEGATIVE reverses the inequality, while keeping the KS3 focus on the representation.
keyRepresentations: Number line with open vs closed circle at the boundary plus an arrow for the solution set
The symbol quartet <, ≤, >, ≥ mapped to circle style and direction
Worded constraint ↔ inequality symbol ↔ number-line diagram triple
A test value checked inside and outside the range
commonMisconceptions: Confuses strict (<, >) with inclusive (≤, ≥): uses the wrong circle style (open for ≥, filled for <).
Shades or points the arrow the wrong way (reads the symbol direction backwards).
Treats the solution as a single boundary value (x < 5 means x = 4) rather than a whole set.
Worded-boundary error: renders 'at least 12' as x > 12 (strict) instead of x ≥ 12.

learn.summary: An inequality compares expressions and, unlike an equation, its solution is a RANGE (a set) of values rather than a single value. On a number line that range is shown by a circle at the boundary — open/hollow for strict < or > (boundary excluded), closed/filled for inclusive ≤ or ≥ (boundary included) — with an arrow or segment covering the values that satisfy it. Solving uses the same inverse operations as equations, except that multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the inequality sign (an extension point). The core skill is translating fluently among a worded constraint, the inequality symbol and the number-line diagram, tying circle style to boundary inclusion, the arrow to the satisfying set, and rehearsing worded phrases such as 'at least' and 'at most'.

activities.title: Build and test a number-line inequality
feedback: If a value exactly on the boundary is marked as satisfying under > or <, ask: 'does the boundary value itself make the statement true?' For strict < or >, it does not, so the circle is open.
If the arrow covers values that fail the test, pick one value on each side (e.g. is −5 ≥ −2? is 0 ≥ −2?) to decide which side belongs to the solution.
If only the boundary point is marked, prompt that an inequality's solution is EVERY value in the range — mark several, then the whole arrow or segment; contrast with an equation's single answer.
activities.rationale: A live builder plus a 'does this value satisfy it?' tester makes boundary inclusion and solution-as-a-set directly observable, and letting the symbol switch recolour the boundary value ties the open/closed convention to a fact about solutions. Testing values on each side addresses reading direction backwards.
sourceClaims: Students have difficulty distinguishing > from ≥ and < from ≤ (whether the boundary is included) — shown graphically by whether a boundary line is dashed or solid, the coordinate-grid analogue of an open vs closed circle on a number line; they also shade/read the wrong side, and reason about the solution as isolated points rather than a whole region/set.
learnerActions: Choose an inequality symbol (<, ≤, >, ≥) and a boundary value, then draw the matching number line: decide whether the boundary circle is open or closed and which way the arrow points.
Test several sample values by asking of each, 'does this value satisfy the inequality?', and mark those that satisfy it (e.g. in one colour) and those that do not (another colour).

Switch the symbol from ≥ to > (or ≤ to <) on the same boundary and observe what changes: the boundary circle hollows, and a value sitting exactly on the boundary flips from satisfying to not satisfying.
Deliberately draw the arrow the wrong way, then test values along it to see that a whole stretch of the line fails the check — confirming direction matters.
Read a given diagram (e.g. a filled circle at −2 with a right-pointing arrow) back into symbols and words.
activities.intendedInsight: Inclusion is not an arbitrary drawing convention: whether the circle is filled depends on whether the boundary value itself is a solution. The arrow/segment represents the whole set of satisfying values, and its direction is fixed by what the symbol means.

activities.title: Translate worded constraints into symbols and diagrams
feedback: If 'at least 1' is rendered as x > 1 or an open circle, ask whether 1 itself is allowed — 'at least' includes the boundary, so x ≥ 1 with a closed circle.
If 'less than 4' is drawn with a closed circle at 4, check whether 4 satisfies 'less than 4' — it does not, so the circle is open.
Confirm the compound case by testing x = 1, x = 4 and a value between: 1 should satisfy, 4 should not, and the between-value should satisfy.
activities.rationale: Worded-constraint translation is the part of the representational skill most prone to slips between strict and inclusive phrasing; rehearsing the phrase→symbol mapping and checking the boundary against the words targets that error directly.
sourceClaims: Students have difficulty distinguishing > from ≥ and < from ≤ (whether the boundary is included) — shown graphically by whether a boundary line is dashed or solid, the coordinate-grid analogue of an open vs closed circle on a number line; they also shade/read the wrong side, and reason about the solution as isolated points rather than a whole region/set.
learnerActions: Translate worded constraints into inequality symbols: 'at least 12' → x ≥ 12, 'at most'/'no more than' → ≤, 'more than' → strict >, 'less than' → strict <.
Build a phrase→symbol reference table and, for each phrase, test the boundary value against the words ('is 12 allowed if you must be at least 12?').
Draw the number-line diagram for a compound statement such as 'x is at least 1 and less than 4' (closed circle at 1, open circle at 4, segment shaded between).
Check your diagram by reading it back into words and comparing with the original statement.
activities.intendedInsight: Everyday boundary phrases map precisely onto strict or inclusive symbols, and testing whether the boundary value is allowed decides between an open and closed circle.

activities.title: Solve a simple linear inequality and plot its solution set
feedback: If the solution is given as a single value, remind that solving an inequality yields a range — plot the whole arrow or segment, not a point.
If a test value inside the range fails the original inequality, recheck the inverse operations step by step.
For the negative-multiplier extension: test an actual value in both the original and transformed inequalities to see that the direction must flip for the solutions to agree.
activities.rationale: The curriculum requires solving linear inequalities and representing the solution set on a number line; tying the solved result back to the diagram reinforces that the solution is a set. The negative-multiplier rule is flagged as an extension rather than the KS3 focus.
sourceClaims: Pupils should 'solve linear inequalities in one variable ... ; represent the solution set on a number line' — this is the Key Stage 4 Algebra statutory statement (at KS3 pupils use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ and inequality notation a < x ≤ b).
learnerActions: Solve a one-step or two-step inequality such as 3x + 1 < 10 using the same inverse operations as an equation (subtract 1, then divide by 3, giving x < 3).
Represent the resulting solution set on a number line with the correct open or closed circle and arrow.
Check the solution by testing a value inside the range and a value outside it.
(Extension) Explore what happens when both sides are multiplied or divided by a negative number, using test values to discover that the inequality direction reverses.
activities.intendedInsight: Solving an inequality mirrors solving an equation, but the answer is a set shown on the number line; special care is needed when multiplying or dividing by a negative because the direction reverses.

activities.title: Reference card: symbols, circles and directions
feedback: If a mapping is wrong (e.g. open circle paired with ≥), re-derive it from the question 'is the boundary value a solution?' rather than memorising.
Encourage pairing the card with an actual drawn example so the reference supports, rather than replaces, building the diagram.
activities.rationale: A static symbol-to-diagram reference supports recall but cannot by itself rehearse constructing or translating an inequality, so it is positioned as a check alongside the building activities.
learnerActions: Match each of <, ≤, >, ≥ to its circle style (open for strict, closed for inclusive) and, for inequalities written with the variable on the left (e.g. x < 3), to the direction of its arrow; notice that 3 > x means the same as x < 3, so the arrow still points left.
Use the card as a check when building or reading diagrams, confirming each choice against whether the boundary value is itself a solution.
activities.intendedInsight: The four symbols map systematically onto circle style; they map onto arrow direction once the inequality is written with the variable on the left (e.g. x ≥ a points right), giving a quick self-check reference.

constraints: A static reference card mapping symbols to circle style and arrow direction supports recall but does not rehearse building, translating or reading inequalities independently; pair it with construction tasks.

Matching, multiple-choice and fill-in-the-blank items can check the representation (e.g. 'open or closed circle for x ≥ 3?', 'at least 12 → x __ 12') but recognition-style responses do not elicit independent construction of a diagram or translation; include tasks where the learner draws the number line and states the inequality themselves.
This content lives on a one-dimensional number line, so a three-dimensional representation carries no extra spatial payload for it; a 2D line with circle, arrow and test values is sufficient.
The negative-multiplier direction-reversal rule is a KS4 extension; keep the KS3 focus on the representation and translation.
Keep the solution-as-set idea explicit: an inequality's answer is every value in the range, contrasted with an equation's single value.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The two cited sources support the existence of the boundary-inclusion/direction/set misconceptions and the curriculum requirement to represent solution sets on a number line; they do not establish the comparative efficacy of any specific activity format, interaction, or medium.

The curriculum source labels the solve-and-represent statement as KS4 Algebra (KS3 covers the symbols/notation); activity 3 treats the full solving plus negative-multiplier reversal as an extension beyond the KS3 representation focus, consistent with the source.

Self-audit: the worked values (x ≥ −2 with closed circle and right arrow; compound 1 ≤ x < 4 with closed circle at 1, open at 4) are internally consistent, and 3x + 1 < 10 solves to x < 3 via one-/two-step inverse operations. The negative-multiplier reversal is genuine inequality mathematics, not a spurious denominator-style 'flip'. No arithmetic or logic errors were found in learner-facing text.

probeDeeper: You showed x ≥ −2. Is −2 itself a solution? What about −2.5? How does your diagram say so?
If the circle at −2 were hollow instead of filled, what would change about the inequality?
In your diagram for 'at least 1 and less than 4', is x = 4 included? Is x = 1? How can you tell from the circles?
Are 'you must be more than 12' and 'you must be at least 12' the same inequality? Show each on a number line.
assess.correctAnswer: The diagram shows x ≥ −2 (closed circle = boundary included; arrow to the right = values greater than or equal to −2). The produced number line has a CLOSED circle at 1, an OPEN circle at 4, and the segment between them shaded: 1 ≤ x < 4.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses strict with inclusive circle style — reads the filled circle as x > −2, or draws an OPEN circle at 1 for 'at least 1' / a closed circle at 4 for 'less than 4'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'does −2 itself count as a solution?' — if yes, fill the circle; translate the symbol into words to separate > from ≥.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The wrong circle style appears on read or draw; the boundary's inclusion does not match the symbol/words.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the direction backwards — takes a closed circle with a right arrow as x ≤ −2, or shades the wrong side of the boundary
errorPatterns.nextMove: Test a value on each side (is −5 ≥ −2? is 0 ≥ −2?) to fix which side belongs to the solution.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The arrow/shading covers the values that do NOT satisfy the inequality.

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats the solution as a single value, not a set — marks only a dot at the boundary, or gives one number for x ≥ −2
errorPatterns.nextMove: An inequality's solution is EVERY value in the range — mark several, then the arrow/segment; contrast with an equation's single answer.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws a point with no arrow/segment, or answers 'x = 1'.

errorPatterns.pattern: Worded-boundary translation error — renders 'at least 1' as x > 1 (strict) rather than x ≥ 1, or 'less than 4' as ≤ 4
errorPatterns.nextMove: Build a phrase→symbol table ('at least'→≥, 'at most'→≤, 'more/less than'→ strict) and test the boundary value against the words.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses strict symbols/open circles for 'at least/at most', or inclusive for 'more/less than'.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot read the circle/arrow, uses the wrong circle style, or marks a single point instead of a set.
responseLevels.full: Reads the diagram as x ≥ −2, produces the compound 1 ≤ x < 4 with correct open/closed circles and a shaded set, and justifies each boundary's inclusion against the words — translating fluently in both directions and to a new, compound case.
responseLevels.partial: Reads and draws simple one-boundary inequalities with the correct circle style, but slips on direction, on the 'at least/at most' wording, or on the compound two-boundary case — handles single translations without coordinating symbol, words and diagram across the whole set.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a number line with a FILLED (closed) circle at −2 and an arrow pointing to the right. First: what inequality does this diagram show? Then, on a fresh number line, show the solution to the statement 'x is at least 1 and less than 4'.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Reading the diagram tests whether the child maps a filled circle to ≥ (not >) and a right arrow to 'greater'; producing the compound diagram reverses the translation and exposes both the strict/inclusive choice (closed at 1 for 'at least', open at 4 for 'less than') and whether the solution is drawn as a set (a shaded segment) rather than isolated points. A child who confuses the circle styles or marks a single point cannot produce the correct diagram.
